statement: The net in the picture is folded into a cube. At each corner of the cube, three faces meet. What is the largest possible total of the three numbers that meet at one corner?

figure.alt: A cube net of six squares. Four squares form a row, labelled 6, 1, 5 and 2 from left to right. A square labelled 4 is attached above the square labelled 1, and a square labelled 3 is attached below the square labelled 2.

choices.misconception: I found the smallest corner total, 1 + 3 + 5, instead of the largest.
I only looked at points where three squares already meet in the flat net, and the best of those was 6 + 1 + 4.
I saw that 6 and 5 are opposite, so I took 6 with the next biggest numbers, 4 and 3, without checking that 4 and 3 are opposite too.
I added the three biggest numbers, 6, 5 and 4, without checking that 6 and 5 land on opposite faces.

hints: First find which faces end up opposite each other.
Opposite faces never meet at a corner. Every corner uses exactly one face from each pair of opposite faces, so find the three opposite pairs first.
In the row of four, squares two apart fold to opposite faces: 6 with 5, and 1 with 2. That leaves 4 and 3 as the last pair.

solutions.reliable: In a row of four squares, the first and third fold to opposite faces, and so do the second and fourth, so 6 is opposite 5 and 1 is opposite 2. The two remaining squares, 4 and 3, are opposite each other. Each corner of the cube touches one face from each opposite pair, and every such choice of three faces meets at a corner. So the largest total takes the larger number from each pair: 6 + 2 + 4 = 12. The transferable idea: on a cube, three faces meet at a corner exactly when no two of them are opposite.

whyOnTest: Net questions test whether you can find opposite faces before folding, because opposite faces can never share a corner.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
